Wow that repo is pathological. On a fresh clone, `git status` took 30 seconds, and printed a warning saying it took 20 seconds just to enumerate untracked files (and offered flags that disables the untracked files tests).

This definitely seems like an issue with the `git_status` module. Keeping the other git modules at their default is fine, and simply disabling `git_status` makes starship nice and zippy.

I'm also hitting this on my own repo, but it's not nearly so pathological. `fish_git_prompt` takes 570ms while warm. Running `git status` by itself actually takes slightly longer at about 660ms, though `git status -s` is around 480ms. And starship is taking about 1.1s (going up to 2s on the first prompt). Most of the time `fish_git_prompt` takes is in the command `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard --directory --no-empty-directory --error-unmatch -- :/ >/dev/null 2>&1` (which is testing for untracked files, and which appears to be what `git status -s` is running as well).

So I'm wondering why starship is taking so much longer to do basically the same thing. It's really only untracked files that should be expensive (since it requires walking the whole work tree), everything else is cheap.

It would be great to have git functionality (and ideally for all the other terminal status providers too!) similar to https://github.com/sindresorhus/pure, which does git status checks completely in the background asynchronously. The terminal remains completely usable and unblocked while the git command is running, and the prompt is simply updated in place when the git result is available.

I recently switched back to pure because of this, after working in large repos like https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs became painful. Now, there is no discernible lag and the results are shown when they are available, without interrupting anything.

I agree, I think performance is a lot better with git cli.

One thing I've done to fix the performance for my HUGE repos is disable untracked files. I have the following git aliases:

```
[alias]
  fastprompt = !git config --local status.showUntrackedFiles no
  slowprompt = !git config --local --unset status.showUntrackedFiles
  st  = status -sb -unormal
```

For the handful of HUGE repos I have, I run `git fastprompt`, which disables showing untracked files. This will leave them out of my prompt, but the trade-off in performance is very significant. When I do want to display the status, `git st` does use `-unormal` which will display all of the untracked files. If I want to undo this change, `git slowprompt`.

Maybe this will be helpful to others.

I just filed #2912 because starship really should not be using the `status.showUntrackedFiles` flag, it should define its own (perhaps `bash.showUntrackedFiles` for compatibility with the bash/fish prompts). Having said that, I also found another way to speed up `git status` in the normal case, which is to enable the untracked-cache feature. The documentation for this is in `git update-index`, but in short:

* Run `git update-index --test-untracked-cache` to make sure your filesystem supports it. This tests it in the current repo, but the results should apply to your whole filesystem.
* Either run `git update-index --untracked-cache` to enable it for the current repo, or set `core.untrackedCache` to `true`. The latter is preferred, and can also be used to enable this feature for your whole system.
* Alternatively, set the `feature.manyFiles` flag to `true`. This changes the `core.untrackedCache` default to `true` and also sets `index.version=4` for path-prefix compression on the index. Note that index version 4 may not necessarily be supported by alternative git implementations.

In testing on a repo with 27k files and 17k directories, `git status --porcelain=2 --branch` was taking 700–800ms with a warm filesystem cache, but after enabling this feature it now takes ~200ms. This is still slower than if I disable untracked files, but it's a significant improvement.

I have not tested starship's performance here, but starship's current implementation runs `git status --porcelain=2 --branch`. That said, it also uses `--no-optional-locks` and I'm unsure if that affects the untracked cache (or why that flag is used at all, it's meant for background operations and there's no comment on it or an explanation in #2465 or 9198a68d634c33fe5a36e5ace00dc25f92cab955).
